newsitem.title: USA: Iditarod leaders take mandatory rest stops.
newsitem.headline: Iditarod leaders take mandatory rest stops.

text.p: Leaders in the Iditarod Trail Sled Dog Race were resting at the tiny town of Takotna late Wednesday, electing to take their mandatory 24-hour layover at that checkpoint 436 miles into the 1,161-mile course.

Doug Swingley, the 1995 race champion, was the first into Takotna, reaching the checkpoint at 10:48 p.m. local time Tuesday. He was followed within 12 minutes by two-time champions Jeff King and Martin Buser.
They were followed within five hours by other top mushers, including Bill Cotter, DeeDee Jonrowe and Tim Osmar.
The Iditarod began Saturday with a ceremonial run from downtown Anchorage. Timed competition began Sunday, with a restart in the community of Willow.
While past champions and their rivals rested at Takotna, they were passed by three other teams that mushed on to Ophir, a checkpoint 38 miles up the trail.
Mitch Seavey, Peryll Kyzer and Ramey Smyth reached Ophir, an abandoned gold-mining settlement, between 8:35 a.m. and 10:48 a.m. Wednesday.

The race pace has been largely set by King, Buser and Swingley. Swingley, of Lincoln, Montana, in 1995 set the race record of nine days, two hours and 42:19 minutes. King, who also won in 1993, last year won the race in nine days, five hours and 43:13 minutes.
The Swiss-born Buser, of Big Lake, Alaska, won the race in 1992 and 1994.

Swingley told the Alaska Public Radio Network that the leaders will relax and change their pace after the 24-hour break. "It won't be as torrid a pace from here on. It'll be more methodical," he told the radio network.

A second dog died in the race, officials reported. The dog was in the team of Wayne Curtis. The Wasilla, Alaska, musher was reported in a layover at Nikokai, a checkpoint 365 miles into the race, while veterinarians investigated the dog death.
Two of the 53 mushers who began the race have dropped out.
